references.text: The Samaritans refused to welcome Jesus because he was on his way to Jerusalem. This background makes it all the more remarkable that Jesus uses a Samaritan as an example in the parable.
The leper who returned to thank Jesus was a Samaritan, showing that Samaritans could demonstrate gratitude and mercy—a recurring theme in Luke.

The Samaritan woman expresses surprise that Jesus, a Jew, asks her for water, since Jews had no dealings with Samaritans. This highlights the tense relationship between Jews and Samaritans, which makes the point of the parable so powerful.

Jews used the word 'Samaritan' as an insult against Jesus. This shows the deep hostility between the groups, adding extra weight to the fact that it is precisely a Samaritan who is the hero of the parable.
Jesus was moved with deep compassion (ἐσπλαγχνίσθη) for the widow in Nain, using the same Greek word applied to the Samaritan. This shows that the Samaritan's compassion reflects Jesus' own mercy.
Jesus was moved with deep compassion (ἐσπλαγχνίσθη) when he saw the crowds, using the same Greek word as describes the Samaritan's reaction when he saw the injured man.
Jesus was moved with deep compassion (ἐσπλαγχνίσθη) when he saw the great crowd, and he healed the sick among them. The same word is used for the Samaritan's pity.
Jesus says 'I have deep compassion for the people' (σπλαγχνίζομαι)—the same word for profound mercy that characterizes the Samaritan's response in the parable.
The father in the parable of the prodigal son was moved with deep compassion (ἐσπλαγχνίσθη)—the same word used for the Samaritan, showing God's merciful character.

Background on the Samaritans as a people: they were descendants of the nations that the Assyrian king settled in Samaria, and they mixed their worship. This explains the Jewish contempt for Samaritans.

Samaritans (men from the northern kingdom) showed mercy to captives from Judah, anointed them, clothed them, and brought them to Jericho—a striking parallel to the good Samaritan on the road to Jericho.
